design_detail: Update of the authors' 2017 systematic review (59 studies) of gabapentin and pregabalin misuse, abuse and overdose, with a qualitative (narrative) synthesis and no meta-analysis. PubMed was searched for studies published 29 July 2016 to 31 August 2020 (four searches); ClinicalTrials.gov and the Cochrane Library were searched for ongoing studies or similar reviews; reference lists of included studies were screened. 55 studies were included: 46 observational studies (Table 1) and 10 case reports or series (Tables 2 and 3; one manuscript counted in both). 29 came from North America (28 USA), 17 Europe, 6 Asia (4 Jordan), 3 Australia; 20 studied gabapentin only, 18 pregabalin only, 17 both. Results are grouped by theme: extent of misuse, effects sought, risk factors, patterns, harms, and the role of health professionals and policy.
can_establish: What studies published between mid-2016 and August 2020 reported about gabapentin and pregabalin misuse: how often non-prescribed use was found in particular groups (mostly people in opioid treatment or detoxification), which effects and motives people described, and which harms were recorded alongside these drugs in poison-centre, death, hospital and insurance data.
cannot_establish: How common misuse is in the general population or among people prescribed these medicines (nothing is pooled, and most samples are people with substance use disorders or records without a denominator of exposed people); that gabapentinoids cause the deaths and hospital stays recorded with them (almost all involved other drugs, mostly opioids, and confounding is not appraised); or that the evidence is complete (one bibliographic database, English only, no appraisal tool).

sample.recruitment: Database search: PubMed (229 records), Cochrane Library and ClinicalTrials.gov (0 records each) and reference lists of included studies (29 records), for 29 July 2016 to 31 August 2020 (PDF p. 2, 2.1; PDF p. 3, Fig. 1). The included studies drew on opioid maintenance clinics, detoxification wards, a syringe service programme, a prison system, community pharmacies, poison centres, ambulance and emergency-department records, post-mortem toxicology and coroners' records, insurance claims and national prescription registers (Table 1, PDF pp. 4–19).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: articles with original experimental or observational data on gabapentinoid abuse (defined as non-therapeutic use to achieve desired physical or psychological effects), misuse (intentional use for therapeutic reasons in a way other than prescribed) or overdose. Excluded: reviews, non-English manuscripts and animal studies (PDF p. 2, 2.2), and at full text, studies already in the 2017 review (3) (PDF p. 3, Fig. 1).
sample.demographics: Not summarized across studies. The six misuse case reports: median age 39 years (range 24–51), 4 of 6 men, all with psychiatric diagnoses and at least one substance use disorder (one nicotine only), 4 of 6 with opioid use disorder (PDF p. 21, 3.2.1).
sample.attrition: PRISMA (Fig. 1, PDF p. 3, legible): 258 records; 126 duplicates removed; 132 screened; 65 excluded on title and abstract (55 not relevant or review, 9 non-English, 1 animal); 67 full texts; 12 excluded (9 not relevant or review, 3 already in the 2017 review); 55 included. No list of excluded full texts.
sample.selection_effects: One bibliographic database, English only, no grey literature beyond reference lists. The included samples are dominated by people with opioid use disorder or other substance use disorders, decedents and spontaneous adverse-event reports; few studies sampled the general population or people prescribed gabapentinoids for pain. Five of the 46 observational studies are by authors of this review (refs 6, 22, 23, 32, 33; reference list, PDF pp. 30–31). Two nested case-control studies of prescribed gabapentinoids with opioids (Gomes et al., 2017, 2018) were excluded because they did not study abuse or people with substance use disorders, and a Swedish population cohort (Molero et al., 2019) is not among the included studies (no reason given); all three are used in the Discussion (PDF p. 27, 4.5, 3rd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Whatever each included study used: self-report in interviews and surveys; urine, oral-fluid or hair testing; post-mortem toxicology; poison-centre and adverse-event reports; prescription fills above a threshold in claims data ('overuse'); pharmacists' suspicion; arrest records. The review defines abuse and misuse but does not apply its definitions to the included studies, and its Limitations name reliance on surrogate markers of misuse (PDF p. 29, 4.7).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. Single studies report frequency (for example, in a US syringe-service sample of 103 people with opioid use disorder: daily 55%, weekly 24%, monthly 11%, less than monthly 9%; Table 1, PDF p. 5) and that swallowing was the usual route, with snorting and injecting reported by minorities (PDF p. 25, 4.4, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Central to most included studies and not adjusted for at review level: gabapentinoids were mostly used with opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine (PDF p. 25, 4.4, 1st paragraph), and in death records were almost always found with other drugs (for example, every gabapentin-positive overdose death in five US jurisdictions had at least one other drug; PDF p. 28, 4.5.1, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: Varies by study: people without the gabapentinoid prescription or detection within the same cohort or registry (for example opioid-maintenance patients not prescribed pregabalin), population controls in one case-control study (9964 cases, 49,820 controls; Table 1, PDF p. 16), or none (surveys, interview studies, toxicology series, case reports).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Severity of substance use, opioid dose, psychiatric illness and pain are the main candidate confounders of the harm associations; the review does not report which included studies measured or adjusted for them. In the British Columbia case-control study the review's own table notes that psychiatric and substance use comorbidities were higher in cases and may confound the results (Table 1, PDF p. 16).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: In the harm studies the comparison groups also used opioids (for example opioid-maintenance patients without a gabapentinoid prescription, or people prescribed opioids alone).

outcomes.instruments: Prevalence of non-prescribed use or positive tests; self-reported motives, effects, sources and routes; DSM-IV dependence (one survey); overdose death, all-cause mortality, hospital admission and emergency visits (cohort and claims studies); poison-centre outcome categories; detection in post-mortem toxicology.
outcomes.validity_norms: No risk-of-bias tool was applied to the included studies; Table 1 lists each study's limitations, and the review describes its assessment of bias as qualitative (PDF p. 2, 2.2; PDF p. 29, 4.7).
outcomes.operationalization: Abuse: non-therapeutic use for desired effects; misuse: intentional therapeutic use other than prescribed; overdose (PDF p. 2, 2.2). The included studies used proxies such as quantities above the maximum dose in prescription data, sustained overuse in claims data, and detection without a prescription.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Full texts were reviewed by three authors with inclusion by consensus; three authors separately extracted data, which the lead author compiled (PDF p. 2, 2.2). Whether titles and abstracts were screened by more than one person is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates; figures are reported study by study as printed (Table 1; Sections 3 and 4). Non-prescribed or nonmedical pregabalin in opioid-maintenance or detoxification samples: 17.7% (Israel, urine, n=300), 18.8% (Germany, oral fluid, n=388; gabapentin 1%), 10.7% (Italy, hair, among patients not prescribed it), 21% lifetime (Sweden, n=73), 0% (Switzerland, n=109), and 56% lifetime, 47% past year, 23% past 10 days (German detoxification ward, n=253). Claims data: sustained gabapentin overuse in 2.0% of people prescribed gabapentin without opioids and 11.7% with opioids (OR 6.32, 95% CI 5.80–6.89). Harms: pregabalin prescription in Swedish opioid maintenance and overdose death HR 2.82 (1.79–4.43); gabapentinoid co-prescription in opioid agonist treatment and all-cause mortality HR 1.71 (1.33–2.20), drug-related poisoning death HR 1.54 (0.60–3.98); sustained gabapentin overuse with sustained opioid overuse and all-cause hospital admission OR 4.083 (2.582–6.457) against gabapentin without overuse. Poison-centre abuse reports: death 0.4%, major effects 6.1%.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level. The review does not say whether the odds and hazard ratios it reports are adjusted, or for what.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned; the methods are said to follow the protocol of the 2017 review, previously published, and PRISMA (PDF p. 2, 2 Methods).
analysis.selective_reporting: Figures are picked from each study by the reviewers without a stated rule, and several are restated in the text differently from Table 1 (reporting issues). Studies outside the inclusion criteria are brought into the Discussion to support the harm conclusion (Gomes et al., 2017, 2018) alongside one that qualifies it (Molero et al., 2019: no excess unintentional overdose after excluding people with substance use disorders), and only the former shape the conclusions.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A heterogeneous set of 55 mostly observational and descriptive studies, most in people with opioid use disorder or in death and poison-centre records. Non-prescribed pregabalin or gabapentin use was frequent in opioid-treatment and detoxification samples (from 0% to over 50% depending on sample, test and time window); motives ranged from getting high to self-treating withdrawal, anxiety or pain; detection in deaths rose where testing was added, with other drugs, mostly opioids, almost always present; and in people also taking opioids, gabapentinoid prescription or overuse was associated with overdose death, all-cause mortality and hospital admission. The only general-population figure (2.5% lifetime) is cited in the introduction, not taken from an included study.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that misuse is a growing trend "that is causing significant patient harm" (PDF p. 1), and the conclusion calls it an alarming trend (PDF p. 29). Gaps: (1) causal language from associations that are not adjusted at review level and mostly involve opioid co-use; the Discussion itself says the studies linking gabapentinoids to opioid overdose death were not of people misusing them (PDF p. 27) and that harm with prescribed combinations was not limited to misuse (PDF p. 28); (2) the statement that opioid use disorder is the greatest risk factor rests largely on samples drawn from people with opioid use disorder, with few comparisons against people without it; (3) the text restates several Table 1 results incorrectly, in the direction of greater harm from gabapentinoids (benzodiazepine and Z-hypnotic hazard ratios mislabelled; one study's 47.1% presented as a detection rate) (reporting issues); (4) the Discussion reads a proportional reporting ratio from spontaneous reports as showing greater abuse liability for pregabalin (PDF p. 21) and later calls gabapentin's abuse potential similar (PDF p. 29); (5) the Swedish cohort finding of no excess unintentional overdose once people with substance use disorders were excluded (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.91–1.08; PDF p. 27) is not carried into the conclusions. The Limitations are candid (qualitative synthesis only, surrogate markers, samples focused on substance use disorders or overdose; PDF p. 29).

timeline.event: Evoy, Morrison and Saklad, Drugs 77:403–426: the original systematic review (59 studies) that this paper updates (cited as ref 1; no project record yet).
Bonnet and Scherbaum systematic review of how addictive gabapentinoids are (cited by this review as ref 66)
Gomes et al.: prescribed gabapentin with opioids and opioid-related death (nested case-control, Ontario); excluded from this review but used in its Discussion
Gomes et al.: prescribed pregabalin with opioids and opioid-related death; excluded from this review but used in its Discussion
Macleod et al.: UK primary-care cohort of people in opioid agonist treatment; included in this review, which labels it a US study
Bonnet, McAnally and Scherbaum: published letter criticizing this review's causal conclusions and its generalization from opioid-dependent samples
The review authors' reply to that letter (Drugs; DOI 10.1007/s40265-021-01495-0), not among the files read.

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent systematic compilation in the files read of studies on gabapentinoid misuse (to August 2020). Its tables are useful pointers to primary studies, but its text figures must be checked against its own Table 1 and preferably against the primary studies. The association between prescribed gabapentinoids and opioid overdose death rests mainly on the Gomes case-control studies and the Swedish and UK opioid-treatment cohorts, which need their own cards (Gomes and Macleod have them); the critique of the review's causal language (Bonnet et al., 2021) is not answered with new data in the files read.

funding.funder: The authors did not receive funding to complete this study (Declarations, PDF p. 29).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors have no conflicts of interest to disclose (Declarations, PDF p. 29).
funding.affiliations_note: College of Pharmacy, University of Texas at Austin (San Antonio); School of Pharmacy, Duquesne University; School of Pharmacy, Northeastern University; PharmToTable LLC (PDF p. 32). Review authors wrote five of the included observational studies (refs 6, 22, 23, 32, 33) and the 2017 review being updated; a 2018 paper by one author, cited as ref 2, argues for reclassifying gabapentin as a controlled substance. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts of people newly prescribed gabapentin or pregabalin, with and without a history of substance use disorder, that measure non-prescribed use, DSM-5 use disorder, withdrawal and overdose with clear denominators and adjust for opioid dose and the severity of other substance use; and general-population surveys that ask about non-medical gabapentinoid use separately from other medicines.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (any), drugs (gabapentin, pregabalin) and outcomes (abuse, misuse, overdose, each defined) are specified (PDF p. 2, 2.2); the question is descriptive, so there is no comparator.
No registration or protocol is mentioned; the methods are said to follow the 2017 review's published methods (PDF p. 2, 2 Methods).
The Limitations explain including heterogeneous designs: misuse of prescription drugs is illegal and hard to capture with one design, and health records likely underestimate it (PDF p. 29, 4.7).

One bibliographic database (PubMed) with the search terms given, plus ClinicalTrials.gov, the Cochrane Library (both empty) and reference lists, searched to within three months of publication; but non-English manuscripts were excluded without justification and no grey literature was sought. Judged 'no' under the project's reading of item 4 (an unjustified language restriction fails partial yes; decision p-amstar2-item4).
Full texts were reviewed by three authors with inclusion by consensus, but who screened the 132 titles and abstracts, at which stage 65 records were excluded, is not stated (PDF p. 2, 2.2; Fig. 1).
Three authors 'separately extracted' data, compiled by the lead author (PDF p. 2, 2.2); neither double extraction of the same studies nor a consensus step is described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Only the PRISMA counts and grouped reasons for the 12 full-text exclusions (Fig. 1, PDF p. 3).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, country, aim, n, study period, results and limitations, and Tables 2 and 3 describe the cases; how each study defined misuse, who the comparison groups were, and whether estimates were adjusted are not given consistently, and one study's period is missing (Macleod et al.).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No tool. A limitations column per study (Table 1) mentions confounding or convenience sampling for some studies only, and at least one row's limitations belong to other studies (reporting issues); this is not an assessment of confounding and selection bias for each study.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Limitations list heterogeneity, retrospective designs, surrogate markers and samples focused on substance use disorders (PDF p. 29), but the abstract and conclusion state that misuse is causing significant patient harm without discussing confounding by opioid use and substance use severity, and the Discussion's harm section treats associations as effects (PDF pp. 27–28).

The review states that heterogeneity rules out pooling (PDF p. 29) and discusses regional differences (more gabapentin misuse in US studies, more pregabalin misuse in European studies, variation within the USA) as reflecting local prescribing (PDF p. 21, 4.1, 4th paragraph); brief.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding and no conflicts declared (PDF p. 29); the review does not flag that its authors wrote five of the included studies.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items are not met (2, no protocol; 4, one database and an unjustified English-only limit; 7, no list of excluded studies; 9, no appraisal of the included studies; 13, risk of bias not carried into the conclusions), which gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. In practice the review is a useful, well-organized catalogue of what was published from mid-2016 to August 2020, but not a trustworthy summary of how common misuse is or whether gabapentinoids cause harm: nothing is pooled, the samples are mostly people with opioid use disorder, and several figures in its text differ from its own table. Cite it for the existence and range of findings, with each figure checked against Table 1, and cite the primary studies for numbers on the site.

key_findings.finding: 55 studies were included: 46 observational studies and 10 case reports or series (one manuscript in both); 29 from North America (28 from the USA), 17 from Europe, 6 from Asia, 3 from Australia; 20 studied gabapentin only, 18 pregabalin only and 17 both.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); 3 Results, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2); Fig. 1 (PDF p. 3)
key_findings.note: The text writes 55 and 46 in words (Fifty-five, Forty-six).

key_findings.finding: PubMed was searched for 29 July 2016 to 31 August 2020 with four searches; ClinicalTrials.gov and the Cochrane Library gave no records and 29 records came from reference lists; non-English manuscripts (9 records), reviews and animal studies were excluded; 258 records, 132 screened, 67 full texts assessed, 55 included.
key_findings.locator: 2.1; 2.2, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 (PDF p. 3)

key_findings.finding: The introduction cites a lifetime prevalence of gabapentinoid misuse of 2.5% in the general population from a 2013 UK study (ref 5), and, from the 2017 review, misuse rates in populations with substance use disorders of 3–68% for pregabalin and 15–22% for gabapentin.
key_findings.locator: 1 Introduction, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: See the reporting issue on the 2.5%: the same UK survey is cited by Bonnet and Scherbaum (2017) as 1.1% for gabapentin and 0.5% for pregabalin.

key_findings.finding: In opioid-maintenance samples, non-prescribed pregabalin was found in 17.7% (Israel, urine, n=300), 18.8% (Germany, oral fluid, n=388; gabapentin 1%), 10.7% (Italy, hair, among patients not prescribed it) and 0% (Switzerland, self-report and hair, n=109); 21% of 73 Swedish patients reported lifetime nonmedical pregabalin use. In a German detoxification ward (n=253), lifetime, past-year and past-10-day pregabalin use were 56%, 47% and 23%, and 92% of those who had used it had obtained it without a prescription.
key_findings.locator: 3.1.2, 1st paragraph (PDF pp. 3, 20); 4.1, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 21); Table 1 (PDF pp. 9, 13, 16, 17, 19)

key_findings.finding: In US commercial insurance claims, sustained gabapentin overuse (prescription fills above a threshold) was found in 2.0% of people prescribed gabapentin without opioids (n=44,148) and 11.7% of those also prescribed opioids (n=15,335) (OR 6.32, 95% CI 5.80–6.89); in a French national insurance cohort, 12.8% of people prescribed pregabalin (n=8692) and 6.6% of those prescribed gabapentin (n=1963) showed possible misuse, and after a first misuse episode 11.6% (gabapentin) and 10.7% (pregabalin) developed a 'primary addiction', a term the review does not define; among Belgian patients treated for substance use disorders who obtained gabapentin, 10% obtained a quantity possibly indicating abuse, against 9.8% of other patients.
key_findings.locator: Table 1: Driot et al. [20] (PDF p. 10), Peckham et al. [33] (PDF p. 15), Van Baelen et al. [42] (PDF p. 18); 4.3, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 25)

key_findings.finding: Motives reported: in Swedish opioid maintenance, relief of emotional problems 65%, getting high 27%, relief of physical problems 12%; in a German detoxification ward, easing opioid withdrawal (67.1% in the text, 61.7% in Table 1) or benzodiazepine withdrawal (6.3%), combining with other substances (51.9%), recreation (46.8%), curiosity (40.5%), mental health problems (13.9%) and pain (8.9%); among US people with opioid use disorder, reasons for first misuse of gabapentin were getting high (58.1%), no access to their usual drug (29%), boosting other drugs (29%), self-treating withdrawal (25.8%) and pain (16.1%).
key_findings.locator: 4.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1 (PDF pp. 7, 9, 17)
key_findings.note: The US percentages fit a denominator of 31 (18 of 31 = 58.1%; 8 of 31 = 25.8%), not the 49 gabapentin-using participants listed in Table 1; 21% of 73 is about 15 Swedish patients, and the base of their motive percentages is not stated (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: In qualitative studies, euphoria and improved sociability were the non-therapeutic effects most often sought, with intoxicating, activating, sedating, dissociative or amnesic effects also described; others used gabapentinoids to ease withdrawal or cravings, come down from other drugs, ease pain or anxiety or help sleep, or because they are not detected in standard drug screens, easier to get or cheaper.
key_findings.locator: 4.2, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Dependence and withdrawal: 11% of German detoxification patients who had used pregabalin met dependence criteria (DSM-IV according to Table 1); people described withdrawal from pregabalin (for example exhaustion, headaches, anxiety, depression, muscle pain, shivering, insomnia, sweating) and from gabapentin, which participants in one US study called similar to but shorter than opioid or depressant withdrawal; three gabapentin case reports described withdrawal including seizures.
key_findings.locator: 4.5, 4th paragraph (PDF pp. 27–28); Table 1, Snellgrove et al. [38] (PDF p. 17)
key_findings.note: The text says 'study criteria' (PDF p. 27), Table 1 'DSM-IV criteria', and Table 1's limitations add that the study's criteria for misuse are not validated (PDF p. 17).

key_findings.finding: Swedish register cohort of 4501 people in opioid maintenance (999 with pregabalin, 1458 benzodiazepine and 1836 Z-hypnotic prescriptions): pregabalin was associated with overdose death (HR 2.82, 95% CI 1.79–4.43) and all-cause mortality (HR 2.01, 1.38–2.91) but not other deaths (HR 1.16, 0.60–2.25); benzodiazepines with non-overdose death (HR 2.02, 1.29–3.18) and all-cause mortality (HR 1.75, 1.28–2.39) but not overdose death (HR 1.49, 0.97–2.29); Z-hypnotics with overdose death (HR 1.60, 1.07–2.39) but not all-cause mortality (HR 1.28, 0.93–1.75) or other deaths (HR 0.96, 0.59–1.59).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Abrahamsson et al. [9]
key_findings.note: The text restates these hazard ratios incorrectly in two places (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: In a cohort of 12,118 people in opioid agonist treatment, gabapentinoid co-prescription rose from 0.5% (1998) to 12% (2014) and was associated with all-cause mortality (HR 1.71, 95% CI 1.33–2.20) but not with drug-related poisoning death (HR 1.54, 0.60–3.98).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Macleod et al. [29] (PDF p. 13); reference 29 (PDF p. 30)
key_findings.note: The review labels this a US study; its reference list gives UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink and Office for National Statistics data (reporting issue). The figures agree with the project's card sc_macleod_2019.

key_findings.finding: In US commercial insurance claims (796,330 people), sustained gabapentin overuse without opioid overuse was associated with all-cause hospital admission (OR 1.366, 95% CI 1.055–1.769), drug-related admission (OR 1.440, 1.010–2.053) and emergency or inpatient care for altered mental status (OR 1.864, 1.324–2.624), against gabapentin without overuse; with sustained opioid overuse as well: all-cause admission OR 4.083 (2.582–6.457), drug-related admission OR 4.722 (2.665–8.369), altered mental status OR 4.380 (2.312–8.301), and emergency or inpatient care for respiratory depression OR 4.106 (1.753–9.619).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Peckham et al. [6]; 4.5, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 27)
key_findings.note: 'Overuse' was defined from prescription claims; the review does not say whether these odds ratios are adjusted.

key_findings.finding: Among 103 people with opioid use disorder at a Boston syringe service programme, those who reported taking gabapentin above 2,400 mg (the study's cut-off) more often reported having had an opioid overdose than those taking less (91% vs 63%, p=0.001), and 67% felt safer using gabapentin than non-prescribed drugs.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Applewhite et al. [55]; 4.5, 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 27)

key_findings.finding: US poison-centre reports of gabapentinoid abuse rose 4.3-fold (0.0144 to 0.0618 per 100,000) from 2006 to 2014; 31.9% involved a single substance; 0.4% ended in death and 6.1% in major effects. A national estimate of 11,669 US emergency-department visits in 2016 involved nonmedical gabapentinoid use, 88.8% of them with another substance.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Dart et al. [19] (PDF p. 10) and Geller et al. [24] (PDF p. 11); 3.1.4 (PDF p. 20)

key_findings.finding: US death records: gabapentin was found in 22% of 4169 overdose deaths in five jurisdictions (4% where it was not tested routinely, up to 41% in Kentucky), always with at least one other drug (opioids 94%, benzodiazepines 64.1%); in Kentucky, detection in overdose deaths rose from 2.9% (2013) to 33.5% (August–December 2014) after gabapentin was added to routine testing.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Hargrove et al. [25] (PDF p. 11) and Slavova et al. [36] (PDF p. 16); 4.5.1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 28)

key_findings.finding: UK and Finnish death records: prospective testing of 3750 UK post-mortem cases found gabapentin in 3.1% and pregabalin in 6.1% (tramadol 3.2%), and routine screening would have missed 57.6% and 53.7% of them; in Finland, pregabalin and gabapentin were found in 29% and 2.9% of 786 fatal poisonings, without a prescription in 13.1% and 0.9%.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Haukka et al. [26] (PDF p. 12) and Nahar et al. [31] (PDF p. 14); 4.5.1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 28)

key_findings.finding: UK deaths involving gabapentinoids rose from 1 (2009) to 137 (2015), 79% with opioids; in Tayside, Scotland, gabapentinoids were implicated in 39% of drug-related deaths in 2016, and 77.3% of these people had not been prescribed one.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Lyndon et al. [28] (PDF p. 13) and Torrance et al. [62] (PDF p. 18); 3.1.3 and 3.1.4 (PDF p. 20)

key_findings.finding: Australia: 1158 reports of intentional poisoning involving pregabalin, with a 53.8% yearly increase (95% CI 44.0–64.2%) from 2005 to 2016, and 88 pregabalin-associated deaths, of which 1.1% were attributed to pregabalin alone; pregabalin-related ambulance attendances in Victoria rose from 0.28 to 3.32 per 100,000 from 2012 to 2017 (p=0.001), 67.6% with sedative co-ingestion (benzodiazepines 36.6%).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Cairns et al. [15] (PDF p. 8) and Crossin et al. [16] (PDF p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Pregnancy: in a case series of 19 infants exposed before birth to opioids and gabapentin, 78.9% showed a similar set of withdrawal signs and 52.6% needed a gabapentin taper in addition to methadone; a US Medicaid study reported neonatal withdrawal in 11.4% of infants exposed to opioids plus gabapentin against 1.0% with opioids alone (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.26–2.06).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Loudin et al. [52] (PDF p. 24); 4.5, 5th paragraph (PDF p. 28)
key_findings.note: The relative risk cannot be derived from the two percentages (reporting issue).

key_findings.finding: In the Discussion, a Swedish population cohort that is not among the included studies (Molero et al., 2019) found more unintentional overdoses after gabapentinoid prescription (HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.19–1.28) but no difference once people with substance use disorders were excluded (HR 0.99, 0.91–1.08); two excluded nested case-control studies found higher odds of opioid-related death with prescribed gabapentin (OR 1.49, 1.18–1.88) or pregabalin (OR 1.68, 1.19–2.36), and higher odds in their higher prescribed-dose categories (OR 1.58 and 2.51).
key_findings.locator: 4.5, 3rd paragraph; references 7, 8 and 68 (PDF pp. 30–31)
key_findings.note: The case-control figures agree with the project's cards sc_gomes_2017 and sc_gomes_2018; cite those studies, not this review, for them.

key_findings.finding: FAERS reports, October 2012 to December 2016: 576 gabapentin and 58 pregabalin abuse, misuse, dependence or overdose reports, of which 18.4% and 41.4% were fatal (cause of death not determined); proportional reporting ratio for pregabalin against gabapentin 1.77. US studies point to more gabapentin than pregabalin misuse and European studies to more pregabalin misuse, which the authors attribute to local prescribing.
key_findings.locator: 4.1, 1st and 4th paragraphs (PDF p. 21); 4.5.1, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 28); Table 1, Evoy et al. [22] (PDF p. 10)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the harm seen with gabapentinoids taken with opioids was not limited to people with substance use disorders or to misuse, and that high-dose combinations may carry risk even with prescribed use.
key_findings.locator: 4.6, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors call their synthesis qualitative only because the studies are highly heterogeneous, and list limited generalizability (small samples, single sites, samples focused on substance use disorders or overdose rather than the general population), retrospective designs, reliance on surrogate markers of misuse and harm, and the assumption that findings for one gabapentinoid apply to the other.

reporting_issues.issue: Macleod et al. (2019) [29] is labelled a US study in Table 1 and described as covering more than 12,000 US patients in opioid maintenance (3.1.3) and patients in opioid treatment in the USA (4.5), but the review's own reference list gives it as an observational study based on the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink and Office for National Statistics death records.
reporting_issues.consequence: The only gabapentinoid mortality cohort in opioid treatment besides the Swedish one is UK primary-care data, not US data; the project's card sc_macleod_2019 agrees. Claims must not cite it as US evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The text misstates the comparison hazard ratios from the Swedish cohort (Abrahamsson et al.). Section 3.1.3 says pregabalin raised opioid-overdose death and all-cause mortality by a magnitude similar to benzodiazepines (HR 2.02 and 1.75), but in Table 1 the 2.02 is the benzodiazepine hazard ratio for non-overdose death, and benzodiazepines were not associated with overdose death (HR 1.49, 0.97–2.29). Section 4.5 gives Z-hypnotics' overdose risk as HR 1.28 (0.93–1.75), which Table 1 gives as their all-cause mortality; Z-hypnotics' overdose-death HR was 1.60 (1.07–2.39).
reporting_issues.consequence: Read with Table 1, the Swedish cohort found overdose-death associations for both pregabalin and Z-hypnotics, not for pregabalin alone; the text's claim that pregabalin's overdose risk was higher than that of benzodiazepines and Z-hypnotics compares hazard ratios with overlapping intervals and, for Z-hypnotics, the wrong outcome. Use Table 1 or the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Tharp et al. [40] studied 104 deaths in which gabapentin was already found in the blood; Table 1 reports gabapentin as directly involved in 47.1% of these deaths and prescribed in 91.4%. The text instead says gabapentin was identified in 47.1% of 104 post-mortem toxicology reports (3.1.4) and in 47.1% of Virginia post-mortem toxicology analyses (4.5.1).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 47.1% is the share of gabapentin-positive deaths in which pathologists judged gabapentin directly involved, not a detection rate among deaths in general; the text's wording overstates how often gabapentin appears in deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The French national cohort with 12.8% possible pregabalin misuse and 6.6% gabapentin misuse is Driot et al. (2019), ref 20 in Table 1 and the reference list, but the text cites it as ref 47 (3.1.1; 4.1), which is a 2016 case report by Driot and colleagues of one woman with pregabalin use disorder. Section 3.1 also lists ref 47 among the observational studies, giving 47 references for 46 studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; readers following ref 47 reach a single case report. The population figures and risk factors come from ref 20.

reporting_issues.issue: For the German detoxification survey (Snellgrove et al. [38]), Table 1 gives the share whose main reason was relieving opioid withdrawal as 61.7%, while the Discussion gives 67.1%.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two is a transposition; which one cannot be told from the review. Cite the primary study.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 4.1 reads the proportional reporting ratio of 1.77 (pregabalin against gabapentin, FAERS spontaneous reports) as indicating that pregabalin has a greater abuse liability, while Section 4.6 states that gabapentin appears to have an abuse potential of similar magnitude to pregabalin; Table 1's own limitations for that study say prevalence cannot be established from spontaneous reports.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review contradicts itself on which drug is more prone to misuse, and a reporting ratio from spontaneous reports measures neither abuse liability nor frequency; do not cite either statement as a finding.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's limitations column cannot be relied on row by row: the Mutschler et al. [30] row (country Switzerland, hair testing in living patients) lists a small sample from Sweden and the limits of post-mortem toxicology; the Geller et al. [24] row reports national estimates of emergency visits while listing as a limitation that the small sample of hospitals precludes state or national estimates.
reporting_issues.consequence: The per-study limitations, the review's only appraisal of its included studies, contain entries copied from other studies or contradicting the row's results.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction's general-population lifetime prevalence of 2.5% (ref 5, Kapil et al., 2014) does not match how Bonnet and Scherbaum (2017, Table 1, PDF p. 5) report the same survey of 1500 adults in England and Wales: lifetime misuse of baclofen 1.3% (19 people), gabapentin 1.1% (17) and pregabalin 0.5% (8). Bonnet's percentages for frequency and source (5 people = 13.1%, 22 = 57.8%) imply a base of about 38 people, which is 2.5% of 1500, and even if no one misused both drugs, gabapentin or pregabalin misuse covers at most 25 people (1.7%) (editors' arithmetic and inference).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 2.5% appears to count lifetime misuse of any of baclofen, gabapentin or pregabalin; it should not be cited as the general-population prevalence of gabapentinoid misuse without the primary paper. The site's only general-population figures in the files read are 1.1% (gabapentin) and 0.5% (pregabalin) lifetime misuse in one online survey.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 4.5 reports neonatal withdrawal in 11.4% of infants exposed to opioids plus gabapentin against 1.0% with opioids alone, with RR 1.61 (1.26–2.06); the crude ratio of these percentages would be about 11 (editors' arithmetic), and the review does not say that the RR is adjusted or for what.
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither the absolute nor the relative figure can be cited from this review; the primary study (Huybrechts et al., 2017, BMJ) is needed. Pregnancy answers wait for a person in the machine lane.

reporting_issues.issue: Claims-data 'overuse' (sustained prescription fills above a threshold, as Table 1 calls it) is described in the text as gabapentin misuse or abuse (3.1.3; 4.3), and the 4.3 sentence gives the two rates as '2.0% vs 11.7%' after saying misuse was more frequent in people prescribed opioids, the reverse order. Section 4.1's figure that 2–8% of all people prescribed gabapentin obtained quantities indicating misuse is attributed to ref 32, whose Table 1 row contains no such figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: A prescription-quantity proxy is presented as misuse; the 2–8% cannot be checked within the review.

reporting_issues.issue: Smaller inconsistencies between text and Table 1: the UK interview frequencies (once 10/19, rarely 5/19, weekly 3/19, daily 3/19) sum to 21, matching the 21 people who had used pregabalin (19) or gabapentin (2) in Table 1, not 19; weekly testing in German opioid maintenance found 43.2% positive all four weeks, which 4.4 calls half of the patients; methadone patients' pregabalin detection is 25% in 3.1.2 and 25.8% in Table 1 and 4.3; the Belgian study period is 2008–2014 in Table 1 and the text but 2011–2014 in the reference title; the first-misuse motive percentages for Buttram et al. [57] fit 31 respondents, not the 49 listed (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor individually; together they show that numbers should be taken from Table 1, and preferably from the primary studies, not from the review's text.
